sections.content: If you've been searching for an affordable, high-potential real estate market, Dayton, Ohio deserves a serious look. While cities like Columbus and Cincinnati grab most of the headlines, savvy investors have been quietly stacking deals in Dayton for years. With median home prices well below the national average, a growing job base, and strong rental demand from students and working-class families, the real estate deals in Dayton OH are among the best in the Midwest right now. Whether you're just getting started or you're a seasoned wholesaler looking to expand your portfolio, this guide will walk you through everything you need to know. If you're new to the game, bookmark our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide as a companion resource.
Dayton OH Real Estate Market Overview

Dayton is a mid-sized city in southwestern Ohio with a population of around 140,000, but the greater Dayton metro area stretches to nearly 800,000 residents across Montgomery, Greene, and Warren counties. Historically an industrial and manufacturing hub, Dayton has been diversifying its economy over the past decade. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base — one of the largest military installations in the country — anchors the local economy and employs roughly 30,000 people. Add in major employers like Premier Health, CareSource, and a growing tech sector, and you have a workforce that needs housing.

Home prices in Dayton remain extremely accessible compared to national benchmarks. As of 2024, the median home price in the city of Dayton sits around $115,000 to $130,000, though prices in surrounding suburbs like Kettering, Beavercreek, and Oakwood run higher — often between $200,000 and $350,000. This wide price range creates opportunities for investors at every level, from budget wholesale deals in the $40,000–$70,000 range to value-add flips in more desirable zip codes. You can explore current inventory and deal flow on our dedicated [Dayton OH market page](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dayton-oh).
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Dayton

Not all Dayton neighborhoods are created equal for investing purposes. Your strategy — whether you're wholesaling, flipping, or holding for rental income — should heavily influence which zip codes you target. Here's a breakdown of the most investor-friendly areas.
High-Volume Wholesale Neighborhoods

items: Westwood and Wolf Creek: High concentration of distressed properties with low acquisition costs. Median prices often fall between $40,000 and $75,000, making it a prime wholesale territory.
Trotwood: A suburb just northwest of Dayton with significant older housing stock, motivated sellers, and strong cash buyer demand from local landlords.
East Dayton (including Belmont): Transitional neighborhoods with pockets of opportunity. Watch for properties near the University of Dayton for student rental upside.
Dayton View: An older, established neighborhood where pre-foreclosures and probate deals surface regularly.

sections.content: Best Areas for Fix-and-Flip Deals

items: Kettering: A stable suburb with strong resale values and buyer demand. ARVs in Kettering frequently range from $180,000 to $260,000, offering solid flip margins on the right acquisition.
Oakwood: One of Dayton's most affluent suburbs with beautifully renovated homes selling quickly. Higher acquisition costs but strong ARVs above $300,000.
Springboro and Centerville: Fast-growing suburban markets with excellent schools, pulling in buyers from Columbus and Cincinnati. Great for higher-end flips.
South Park Historic District: An up-and-coming urban neighborhood with young professional buyers and appreciation momentum.

sections.content: Top Rental Markets in the Dayton Metro

items: Fairborn: Located next to Wright-Patterson AFB, Fairborn has extremely stable rental demand from military personnel and civilians. Average rents for a 3-bed sit around $1,100–$1,350/month.
Huber Heights: A large planned community with working-class families and strong occupancy rates. Entry prices are reasonable with consistent cash flow.
Harrison Township: One of the most affordable buy-and-hold markets in the metro with gross rental yields sometimes exceeding 12–15% on low-priced acquisitions.
Riverside: Military-adjacent community with low vacancy and steady demand, particularly for single-family rentals under $150,000.

Knowing your MAO (Maximum Allowable Offer) before you make an offer is non-negotiable in a competitive market.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Dayton OH
Dayton's market supports multiple investing strategies simultaneously, which is part of what makes it so attractive. Here's how each approach plays out locally.
Wholesale Deals

Dayton is one of the more active wholesale markets in Ohio. The combination of aging housing stock, absentee landlords, and motivated sellers creates a steady pipeline of off-market deals. Typical wholesale assignment fees in Dayton range from $5,000 to $20,000 depending on the property and ARV. The key is building a strong cash buyer list early — there are active fix-and-flip investors and landlords throughout the metro who are always looking for inventory. If you want to sharpen your sourcing skills, our guide on [How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) covers the best methods in detail. For those brand new to the strategy, [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) is a great place to start.
Fix-and-Flip Deals

Flipping in Dayton can be highly profitable when you buy in the right zip code and control your renovation costs. A typical flip scenario in Kettering might look like this: purchase at $110,000, invest $45,000 in renovations, and resell at $220,000 — netting a gross profit around $65,000 before financing and holding costs. Margins shrink fast if you overpay or under-estimate rehab, so disciplined deal analysis is critical. Check out [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals) for a step-by-step breakdown of evaluating flip deals.
Buy-and-Hold Rental Properties

Dayton's rent-to-price ratios make it one of the stronger cash flow markets in the country. A single-family home in Harrison Township purchased at $65,000 might rent for $875–$950 per month, delivering a gross yield north of 15%. Even in more stabilized areas like Huber Heights, investors are finding 3-bedroom properties at $130,000 that rent for $1,200–$1,400/month. The 1% rule — where monthly rent equals at least 1% of the purchase price — is actually achievable in many Dayton zip codes, which is rare in today's market.
Local Market Trends to Watch in 2024

items: Rising rents with low vacancy: Dayton's rental vacancy rate has dropped below 5% in several submarkets, pushing average rents up 6–9% year-over-year in 2023.
Increased out-of-state investor interest: Investors from California, New York, and Texas are discovering Dayton's cash flow potential, creating more competition for the best deals.
Downtown revitalization: The Water Street District and Oregon Historic District are driving urban interest and pushing appreciation in adjacent neighborhoods.
Military housing demand: Ongoing expansion at Wright-Patterson AFB continues to fuel rental demand in Fairborn, Riverside, and Beavercreek.
Aging housing stock = deal flow: Over 60% of Dayton's housing units were built before 1970, meaning motivated sellers, estate sales, and renovation opportunities aren't going away anytime soon.

Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Dayton OH
Dayton's affordability is attracting investors from higher-cost markets across the country. If you're considering investing remotely, here's what you need to know before you wire any money.

items: Build a local team first: You need a reliable property manager, a licensed contractor with rehab experience, and a local real estate attorney. Don't skip this step — remote investing lives or dies by your team.
Visit before you scale: Fly in for a weekend. Drive the neighborhoods you're targeting. What looks fine on Zillow may be a very different story in person, especially in transitional areas.
Understand Dayton's micro-markets: A street-by-street difference in Dayton can mean the difference between an A-class rental and a property you can't keep tenanted. Local knowledge matters.

Use data-driven tools to screen deals remotely: Platforms like AIWholesail let you filter distressed properties, run comps, and identify motivated sellers without being on the ground — invaluable for out-of-state investors.

Focus on neighborhoods near major employers: Properties within 10–15 minutes of Wright-Patterson AFB, Premier Health campuses, or the University of Dayton have built-in demand drivers that reduce your vacancy risk.

Account for Ohio's property taxes: Montgomery County property taxes average around 1.5–2% of assessed value annually. Factor this into your cash flow analysis — it's higher than some investors expect.

Start with turnkey or light rehab before heavy value-add: If you're new to the Dayton market, reduce your execution risk by targeting properties that need cosmetic work rather than full gut renovations until you have a proven contractor in place.

sections.content: Pro Tip: When analyzing any Dayton deal remotely, always order an independent inspection even if the seller provides one. Dayton's older housing stock frequently has hidden issues — aging electrical panels, cast iron drain lines, and foundation concerns — that can blow up your rehab budget if missed. Budget a contingency of 10–15% on top of your contractor estimate.
How to Find Real Estate Deals in Dayton OH

Finding good deals in any market comes down to your sourcing strategy. In Dayton, the most effective approaches include direct mail to absentee owners and pre-foreclosure lists, driving for dollars in target neighborhoods, connecting with local wholesalers and bird dogs at REI meetups, and pulling probate and estate records from the Montgomery County Probate Court. Many of the best deals in Dayton never hit the MLS — they move through private networks. That's why a strong off-market sourcing strategy is essential, and exactly why tools that surface motivated seller data can give you a significant edge in this market.
